source.title: Learning from Emergence: A Study on Proactively Inhibiting the Monosemantic Neurons of Artificial Neural Networks
source.authors: Jia-Chuan Wang; Shimin Di; Lei Chen; Charles Wang Wai Ng

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies a statistical proxy for neuron monosemanticity and interventions on it, but does not measure the share of neurons with one or two human-named jobs, test explanations on held-out activations, or test the other listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports proxy-monosemanticity measurements and illustrative Pythia neuron results, recorded below as findings about the subject that none of the listed versions specifically measure. Its GLUE, ImageNet, and HKO-7 task scores evaluate the proposed training method, not the listed interpretability claims, so they are omitted. The paper itself notes that monosemanticity lacks a unified definition and that its feature-independent metric is a proposed proxy.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes a feature-free statistical proxy (Monosemantic Scale) and a training-time inhibition method (Reverse Deactivation), evaluated on benchmark accuracy. It never audits what share of neurons have one human-namable job. It does not score explanations, examine InceptionV1, compare interpretability across tools or architectures, or build neuron attribution graphs. The Pythia French-neuron examples are selected illustrations using sparse probing; they report loss effects, not interpretability shares. None of V1–V7 is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors hypothesize that fewer monosemantic neurons drive performance gains with scale. They propose an online proxy metric and Reverse Deactivation, and report small benchmark gains on GLUE, ImageNet and HKO-7 (p<0.1). They also report that Reverse Deactivation lowers the proxy while naive deactivation raises it. Larger Pythia models showing smaller loss from ablating a French neuron is offered as motivation, not as a main result.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes an online statistical proxy and a training-time neuron inhibition method; it does not reproduce the audit or explanation-testing recipes in the listed sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The Pythia neuron-deactivation effect is reported to weaken as model size increases. The Swin-B decrease-ratio result is small and depends on the inhibition method.

fits_no_version.finding: In Pythia-v0, ablating a probe-identified French neuron raises loss mainly on French inputs, and less in larger models (figure only).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The causal importance of individual feature-selective neurons declines with model scale.

fits_no_version.finding: On Swin-B, Reverse Deactivation lowers the proxy Monosemantic Scale slightly (0.013% vs 0.003% original), while naive deactivation raises it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training-time inhibition can shift a statistical activation-sparsity proxy for monosemanticity.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 30th ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD ’24)
record.problems: The paper acknowledges that monosemanticity lacks a unified definition. Its proposed Monosemantic Scale is a statistical proxy that does not use human-labeled semantic features, so it does not establish how many neurons have a human-namable job. The Pythia examples concern selected neurons and give no numerical values in the text; the Swin-B validation reports averages over 10k neurons without uncertainty estimates. The authors state that experiments on very large models were beyond their resources.
record.rows_left_out: Task performance results in Tables 1–3 and 5–8 are omitted because they evaluate the proposed training method’s benchmark performance rather than neuron job shares, explanation fidelity, or another listed version.

untested.parts: No audit of neuron job shares in Qwen3-32B or any model.
No job-share estimates across models or scale; the Pythia scale comparison concerns ablation loss only.
No analysis of InceptionV1 or canonical polysemantic neurons.
No comparison of interpretable shares across tools, architectures or regularization.
No held-out prediction test of explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's 'monosemantic' is a statistical deviation score, not a human-interpretable job, so it has no bearing on the essay's interpretability shares. It cites Bills et al. only in passing. The record's judgement of T6/discusses is acceptable.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit neuron poles for one-job, two-related-jobs, or not-understood shares.
Does not report comparable job-share estimates across dense or mixture-of-experts language models, or at trillion-parameter scale.
Does not analyze the InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron or recursive generalization.
Does not compare interpretability rates across architectures, regularization, or explanation tools, or estimate rates for InceptionV1-sized vision models.
Does not test attribution graphs built from a model’s own neurons.
Does not test whether explanations fit activating examples but fail to predict other firing locations.
Does not score neuron explanations by simulated activations on new text.
